question: The Federal Aviation Authority of the United States (FAA) has recently issued a notice introducing the category ‘unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) (Notice N7110.800)1’ in its reporting systems for aviation professionals. The German Luftfahrt-Bundesamt officially refers to a reporting platform run by the University of Würzburg’s department for aerospace technology for it to investigate UAP scientifically.

UAP and unknown drones may pose safety risks for civil aviation. The Commission has confirmed (E-002267/2025(ASW))2 that the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EUASA) and national civil aviation authorities may receive safety reports under Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 of 3 April 2014 on the reporting, analysis and follow-up of occurrences in civil aviation3.

In this context, can the Commission indicate whether the EUASA has reviewed these recent international developments, and what measures could be considered to improve the harmonisation of reporting, and the analysis of such occurrences across Member States and internationally, in line with best practices for aviation safety?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.3.2026) The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) is aware of these developments, which were communicated directly to the Agency and the Commission in 2025.

As explained in the Commission’s replies to questions E-002375/2023, E-000314/2024, E001567/2025 and E-002267/2025, Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs) can be reported, as any other aviation safety occurrences, via a harmonised reporting system at EU level, called ECCAIRS21, already implemented and managed in accordance with Regulation (EU) 376/20142.

The users of ECCAIRS2 are Member States, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, and EASA. These occurrences are classified and stored in the European Central Repository of aviation safety occurrences for further analysis. EASA has confirmed that, at present, the risk situation remains unchanged and that no further action is warranted in this area.
